name: Negative air ionization therapy

lead: Negative air ionization therapy uses a device, an ionizer, to raise the number of negatively charged particles in room air. Users are mostly interested in mood and energy, and some people in appearance-focused communities include it in routines aimed at better sleep, lower stress and a fresher-looking face.

The appearance payoff is indirect: improved mood, sleep and air quality are hoped to translate into a rested look. Research has concentrated on seasonal affective disorder and depression, where high-output devices have been compared with bright light; Wikipedia notes that a 2018 review judged the evidence for therapeutic effects inconsistent.

paras: People place a room ionizer or a small personal unit in the bedroom or workspace and run it for periods through the day. In clinical studies, high-output devices are used in the morning for set sessions, usually alongside or compared with light therapy.

Some ionizers produce ozone as a by-product, which can irritate the lungs, and regulators in some regions limit ozone emissions from air cleaners. Skin or appearance benefits have not been tested directly in published trials.

angle.text: Users run an ionizer in the bedroom or workspace hoping for better sleep and mood and cleaner air, which they associate with fresher-looking skin and a more rested face. Direct effects on appearance have not been studied.

lead: Negative air ionization therapy is the use of air ionizers, devices that add negatively charged ions to indoor air, as a non-drug treatment for low mood, seasonal affective disorder and sometimes respiratory or stress-related complaints [1][2]. Negative ions occur naturally near waterfalls, forests and the sea, and ionizers imitate this with a high-voltage corona discharge or similar methods [1].

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles, ionizers are placed in bedrooms with the hope of better sleep, calmer mood and cleaner air, which proponents link to a rested, healthier-looking face. The link to appearance is a chain of claims rather than a tested effect.

Research has mostly examined mood. Wikipedia describes a randomized trial in seasonal affective disorder in which high-density negative ionization was compared with bright light and low-density ions, and notes that the mainstream scientific community considers many applications of the therapy pseudoscientific, while a 2018 review described inconsistent evidence [2].
infobox: Room ionizers, portable and HVAC units [1]

paras: Negative air ions are oxygen molecules or atoms that have gained an extra electron [1]. Corona-discharge ionizers apply high voltage to sharp electrodes so that air molecules pick up electrons; other designs use piezoelectric cold plasma or ultraviolet light [1]. Devices range from small portable units to room units and ducted HVAC modules [1].
Output density matters in research. Studies distinguish high-density devices, with ion concentrations far above ambient levels, from low-density devices used as an inactive control [1][2].

Proponents say negative ions improve mood, energy and sleep, and that they attach to dust and allergens so that particles settle out of the air [1]. Some also propose changes in serotonin activity as a mechanism, which the source describes as still under investigation [1]. People who use ionizers for appearance goals generally expect these effects to reduce the look of tiredness and stress.

A randomized controlled trial summarized on Wikipedia compared bright light, high-density negative ions and low-density ions in seasonal affective disorder; post-treatment improvement was 57.1% for bright light, 47.9% for high-density ions and 22.7% for low-density ions [2]. A trial in students reported that high-density ions reduced depression scores relative to a low-density placebo [2]. Grokipedia describes a meta-analysis of randomized trials reporting lower depression scores with high-output generators, though results for anxiety and sleep were inconsistent [1]. A 2018 review cited by Wikipedia described the evidence for therapeutic effects as lacking consistency [2]. No published trials were found examining skin or facial appearance.

Some ionizers release ozone, a gas known to irritate the lungs [1][2]. Designs using piezoelectric cold plasma are described as producing less ozone than traditional corona systems [1]. High humidity reduces ion concentrations near a device [1].
